justice: The carriageway is very wide with multiple motor-vehicle lanes, while no dedicated sidewalk is visible on either side, indicating spatial resources are allocated mainly to drivers rather than all road users equally.

The roadside consists largely of narrow unpaved shoulders and vegetated edges, so people walking or cycling appear to have much less safe and usable space than motor vehicles.

safety: The road is straight and has clear centerline and lane markings, which improves forward visibility and helps drivers anticipate oncoming traffic.

The corridor appears open and lightly trafficked in this image, which may reduce immediate conflict, but the wide roadway can also encourage higher vehicle speeds.

livability: The street runs through a green, tree-lined landscape, which provides a pleasant environmental backdrop but does not by itself create an active or socially supportive public realm.
No shops, homes, bus stops, benches, or community destinations are visible, so the corridor appears to offer very little support for daily social life or access to services.
The environment feels quiet and uncluttered, yet its highly transport-oriented design and lack of street-side amenities reduce its usefulness as a place to spend time.
The roadside vegetation adds ecological character, but the absence of human activity or gathering spaces makes the overall livability relatively low.
sustainability: Continuous rows of mature roadside trees on both sides contribute to carbon uptake, shade generation, and some ecological value.
